QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Economists were asked when they saw the low points in the annual rate of inflation as measured by the consumer price index and the underlying rate of inflation.
Most see both measures troughing in either the second or third quarters, and at levels consistent with public pronouncements of the Reserve Bank of Australia.

For the headline rate, a number of economists at the lower end of the forecast range expected a negative June quarter CPI reading, taking the annual rate down towards zero. June quarter data is due to be released on July 23.

The impact of the December official rate cut, and the competition inspired cut earlier this year, will still affect the June quarter result, while the impact from the May 23 official rate reduction will first show up in the September quarter.
The impact of the rise in the Australian dollar in 1996 is also expected to keep the downwards pressure on both the CPI and underlying rates of inflation.
The underlying inflation measure excludes almost 50 percent of the CPI, and as a result is far less volatile.
Accordingly while its trough will be well above the CPI trough, peaks in the underlying rate also tend to be well under the peaks in the CPI.

While the trough may be near, economists said inflation would not accelerate rapidly and for most it would be 1999, on current projections, before the underlying inflation rate threatened the top of the RBA's two to three percent target band.

NEW MOTOR VEHCILE REGISTRATIONS - At the end of a two week data drought, motor registrations data are not expected to be a market mover. But a number of economsts said that while they had been often ignored, registrations may attract some attention this month given the softness seen in retail trade and concerns over declining confidence. Signs of softness in consumer spending on registrations would add to the market belief that a fifth rate cut is on the way.
